title: The Mystery of the Avalanche Gate
markdown:
The wind howled a hungry song around the Whispering Peaks. Granite and heather: that was the rhythm Mae felt in her bones. Oriel, her raven, a smudge of midnight, was always her shadow.

One dawn, snow painted rose and gold, she saw them. Footprints. Not sheep, not fox: deliberate, purposeful. They led from a hidden ravine, across untouched snow, straight to the colossal avalanche gate that sealed the north pass. It was shut. Tightly.

“Oriel. Who opened that gate? And why?” He croaked, low and knowing.

He shot upward, a dark arrow against blinding blue, circled the gate, then plummeted to her finger. “The lock,” he rasped, dry leaves. “It’s new. Not rusted.” Someone had tampered.

A thrill replaced unease. A puzzle the peaks themselves had whispered. Footprints in snow tell stories. These led away from the gate toward the highest, most treacherous ridge.

To follow them she had to climb, and climbing meant the yawning emptiness—her own gnawing fear of heights. Oriel nudged her cheek, a silent feathered reassurance.

“All right. Let’s go.”

They scrambled over loose scree. His sharp caws found the safest holds. The wind whipped her hair; the drop stretched. She focused on each handhold, his calls a guiding melody. Her heart hammered with effort, not only fear.

The tracks ended at a sheltered cleft. By a sputtering fire sat an old shepherd, his face a roadmap of worry, a worn leather pouch clutched close.

“You,” he stammered. “How did you get past the gate?”

“That is what we would like to know. Your footprints were the only ones.”

His shoulders slumped. “I had to. My prize ram, Elara, fell into a deep gully. The gate was the only way to reach her before the wolves. I swore I would mend the lock the moment I returned.” He gestured to the pouch. “Rare herbs. A desperate act. Love.”

Mae looked at Oriel. A knowing nod. Not malice: a fierce care for an animal.

Then a flash of colour. Oriel pecked near the fire: a small brightly coloured scarf. “Elara’s?” Mae pulled it free. It was not wool.

Horror replaced the shepherd’s worry. “Elara would not wear that. That looks like the scarf my granddaughter lost weeks ago when she visited. She must have followed Elara. She is lost out here.”

He had not only opened the gate for a ram. He now feared his own granddaughter was in danger. Panic, the most potent of mountain storms, had driven the hasty decision.

Mae’s fear of heights evaporated into usefulness. She knew these mountains. With Oriel scouting, she guided the shepherd down a hidden descent, a passage only a guide’s daughter would know. The raven swooped and called them to a snow-dusted ledge. There, huddled against the biting wind, was a little girl, the bright scarf clutched in a mittened hand.

Relief. Grateful tears. The shepherd, voice thick, explained everything to Mae’s father. The gate would be secured. He vowed to teach his granddaughter the true risks of the peaks.

Mae stood beside her father as the sun dipped, painting fire and amethyst. A new strength bloomed. She had faced the drop, uncovered a truth born of love and panic, and helped two lost souls home. The Whispering Peaks kept their mysteries. She knew, with a certainty as solid as the granite underfoot, that she could unravel them: a mountain guide’s daughter, resourceful, a true discoverer.
